To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the photophysical properties of the acceptor EYFP and the energy transfer efficiency in the cameleon YC3. 1 are strongly dependent on pH, and the existence of multiple conformations of cal modulin is demonstrated by time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy.
the photophysical properties of EYFP are complex and that time-resolved fluorescence measurements are required to obtain information on energy transfer in the cameleon construct YC3.2.

the fluorescence of EYFP can be described by two species, a protonated species that is excited in the 500-550 nm region and a deprotonated one that is excited in a region of the spectrum that overlaps with the ECFP absorption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the photophysical properties of cameleon proteins, with the aim of improving our understanding of their photophysical behavior and of their potential as Ca(2+) sensors in living cells.
the development of a new class of Ca(2+) indicators based on the green fluorescent protein.

the investigation of the photophysical properties of green fluorescent protein and its derivatives and with the development of time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopic techniques for the investigation of the conformational dynamics of cameleons and of the mechanism of the energy transfer in these proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the YC3.2 cameleon construct is a very sensitive Ca(2+) indicator with an apparent Ca(2+) affinity of 0.3 microM, a high quantum yield, and a large Stokes shift, and that the fluorescence of YC3. 2 is a very sensitive probe for Ca(2+).

the Ca(2+) dependence of the fluorescence of YC3. 1 is a result of the interplay of a number of factors, including changes in the conformation of calmodulin and the excited-state proton transfer in EYFP.

the Ca(2+) concentration-dependent changes in the fluorescence properties of the cameleon constructs are due to the interconversion between two conformations of calbindin, which are in equilibrium and which are dependent on the Ca(2+)/calbindin concentration ratio, and not to the existence of two different calmodulin conformations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the time-resolved spectroscopic data offer more information about the conformational changes of the cameleon protein and the efficiency of the resonance energy transfer than steady-state data.

the Ca(2+) concentration-dependent changes in the efficiency of resonance energy transfer between the donor and the acceptor in the cameleon construct are due to a change in the conformation of the calmodulin domain, which affects both the donor-acceptors distance and the orientation of the transition dipole moment of the donor and acceptor.

the time-resolved measurements provide additional information on the structure of the cameleon constructs, whereas the steady-state measurements provide information on the efficiency of energy-transfer and the extent of energy-transfer in the sample.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the time-resolved spectroscopic data is essential for the correct interpretation of the steady-state fluorescence data obtained for the cameleon constructs.
time-resolved fluorescence measurements provide additional and complementary information to steady-state measurements, which is of particular importance in the case of complex constructs such as YC3.
time-resolved fluorescence is an excellent technique to study the conformational changes that occur in cameleon constructs upon Ca(2+ binding).
